Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Acceptance summary:

The manuscript describe the phenotype when Naa10 and Naa12 are inactivated and how Naa12 compensates Naa10 deficiency, reducing the phenotype observed when Naa10 is inactivated. The finding of a new N-acetyltransferase will be useful to the field of N-terminal acetylation.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Naa12 rescues embryonic lethality in Naa10-Deficient Mice in the amino-terminal acetylation pathway" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Philip Cole as the Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

Mutations in the X-linked gene Naa10, which encodes a major protein N-terminal acetyltransferase, are known to be causative in Ogden syndrome, a genetic disorder associated with infantile death. The manuscript reports that hemizygous knockout of Naa10 in male mice does not cause complete embryonic lethality despite the fact that it is responsible for the acetylation of about 50% of all the proteins. This leads the authors to discover a paralogous mouse gene Naa12 and demonstrate that Naa12 can compensate for Naa10 loss of function and that null mutations in both genes lead to complete embryonic lethality. This is an important finding. The authors also provided a thorough account of the variety of development abnormalities in the Naa10 hemizygous mice at all stages of development. Importantly, the authors identified several phenotypes in the mice that upon further analysis, we also noted in the some patients.

All reviewers are enthusiastic about the finding of a new N-terminal acetyltransferase and think that this is a major strength of the manuscript. In addition, the phenotypical characterization of Naa10 is also useful to the field.

Essential revisions:

Some of the revision recommendations requires additional experiments. The reviewers and the Reviewing Editor have discussed and agree that these additional experiments should only take a few weeks to complete.

1) Carry out an in vitro acetyltransferase assays with Naa12-Naa15 to validate the proposed mechanistic model.

2) Check whether Pax3 and HoxC8 proteins' abundance/stability are affected in NAA10 KO mouse tissue or MEF.

3) Obtain experimental evidence to support that N-terminal acetylation is lost in the double knockouts. If such evidence is not possible or will take too much experimental effort, please tone down the claim that the complete machinery for the process of amino-terminal acetylation of proteins in mouse development is identified.

4) Revise the text according to the comments by all three reviewers to make it easier for readers to understand.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

1) It is important to show that N-terminal acetylation is lost in the double knockouts. Only with that, the authors can conclude that they have identified the "the complete machinery for the process of amino-terminal acetylation of proteins in mouse development."

2) Naa12 is new, so if not done yet, the sequence needs to be deposited into Genbank.

3) The presentation needs to be polished.

i) The title "Naa12 rescues embryonic lethality in Naa10-Deficient 1 Mice in the amino-terminal acetylation pathway" is misleading. When I saw the title, I got the impression that Naa10-dficient 1 mice show embryonic lethality. I would suggest to change it to indicate that Naa10 and Naa12 have redundant roles in embryonic development. Also, "Naa10-Deficient 1 Mice" needs to be changed to "Naa10-deficient mice."

ii) In the impact statement "Mice doubly deficient for Naa10 and Naa12 display embryonic lethality…", the word "doubly " is unnecessary.

iii) Too many acronyms, which make the reading a bit difficult. The terms NTA and Nt-acetylation could be avoided.

iv) At the end of page 9, please cite the sequence alignment in Figure S6.

v) On page 12, "Naa12 may rescue loss of Naa10 in mice" could be more assertive.

vi) Overall, I feel that the authors could polish the manuscript so that the salient points could be conveyed more easily to readers.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

Overall this is a very good paper, but some issues need further attention.

– Authors present data showing that mNAA12 can acetylate some peptides at their N-end, however these reactions are performed with just the monomer and NatA activity is catalysed in vivo by the heterodimer Naa10-Naa15, showing an N-terminal acetylation in vitro activity different to Naa10 and being more similar to the observed in cells. Therefore, it is important to characterize Naa12-Naa15 in vitro enzymatic activity assessing its specificity using diverse NatA described peptidic substrates and compare it with the regular NatA enzymatic complex that presents NAA10 as catalytic subunit.

– There is a clear phenotype when mNAA10 is inactivated however, there is not a dramatic defect in protein N-terminal acetylation as it has been observed in other organisms like yeast and Arabidopsis thailiana. It has been observed by several authors that some proteins stability is affected when they are not N-terminal acetylated influencing the biological activity of these proteins. Authors comment that Pax3 and HoxC8 proteins regulate some of the biological activities deregulated in mice when mNAA10 is inactivated. As both proteins are NatA substrates and their stability could be affected when mNAA10 is inactivated it would be interesting to assess their abundance in NAA10KO embryos, mice tissue and/or MEFs in comparison with the observed in wild-type samples. These results could bring some light to the molecular mechanisms that are governing the effects observed in these mice.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Line 55 of the abstract "Male mice lacking Naa10 show no globally apparent in vivo NTA impairment and, surprisingly, do not exhibit embryonic lethality". This statement is misleading as written (and appears again in the discussion) as later in the paper, the authors describe that homozygous mice were underrepresented at birth, and describe embryonic phenotypes and embryos that underwent lysis by 10.5. Suggest rephrasing to.…do not exhibit complete embryonic lethality.

The fate of the Naa10 mice could be written more clearly. As it stands, there is a vagueness as to the number of mice that were not born, that die as early neonates and the number that survived to adulthood. Authors should consider adding a Kaplan Myer survival curve. Statements like "Some of the Naa10 hemizygous mice survived to 4 months is.." is not helpful.

Given the phenotypic effect of Naa12+/- Naa10 +/-, females, it may have been interesting to access any effects in acetylation?

results.result: Naa10 knockout mice exhibit increased neonatal lethality and pleiotropic developmental defects but do not show complete embryonic lethality. Naa10-/Y mice display developmental delays, growth retardation, and various malformations during embryonic stages (E10.5), with survival rates dramatically decreasing after birth, particularly in the first three days of life. Surviving mutants exhibit multiple phenotypes including hydrocephaly, cardiac defects, homeotic anterior transformation, piebaldism, and urogenital anomalies.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7, C36-C41, and C138 collectively demonstrate that Naa10 KO mice survive to birth but exhibit increased neonatal lethality and diverse developmental abnormalities. The data include quantitative survival analysis (C40: 76.3% lethality by P3), embryonic observations with documented developmental delays and malformations (C36-C38), and phenotypic characterization (C7, C41). The findings are supported by multiple figures (Figure 1A-C) and represent primary experimental observations across two independent Naa10-deficient mouse lines.

results.result: Naa10-/Y mice exhibit severe congenital heart defects including ventricular septal defects (VSDs), double outlet right ventricle (DORV), atrial septal defects (ASDs), and persistent truncus arteriosus (PTA), with patent ductus arteriosus observed in both male and female knockouts. These cardiac malformations are incompatible with postnatal survival and likely explain the neonatal lethality observed in Naa10 KO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 provide detailed quantitative data on cardiac defects at specific developmental stages (E14.5, E18.5, P0) with sample sizes (n=6/28, n=3/28). The inference that these defects explain neonatal lethality (C48, C50) is well-supported by established knowledge (C47) that murine outflow tract defects and VSDs are incompatible with postnatal survival, combined with the observed timing of death. Figure 1D provides histological evidence.

results.result: Naa10 knockout results in reduced body weight and decreased growth rates in both male and female mice. Statistical analysis demonstrates that Naa10-/Y males are consistently the smallest in their litters throughout life, with the knockout reducing both overall weight and growth rate. In females, heterozygous Naa10 KO is sufficient to significantly reduce both weight and growth rate.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 present primary observational data with within-litter comparisons showing statistical significance (C53: p<0.0001; C54: p=0.0079). Claims C127-C128, C130 provide rigorous statistical modeling using generalized estimating equations (GEEs) that account for repeated measurements and confirm the effects on both weight and growth rate. The data are supported by Figure 2A and Figure 7, with appropriate statistical controls for known variability factors.

results.result: Naa10 KO mice exhibit skeletal abnormalities with complete penetrance, including piebaldism (100% hypopigmentation) and bilateral supernumerary ribs (14 pairs instead of 13). The extra ribs transform T8 vertebrae into an anterior T7-like phenotype, and additional skeletal changes include increased sternebrae number, cervical vertebrae fusion (C1/C2), and anterior transformation of the first sacral vertebra to a lumbar-like phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C61 describe skeletal phenotypes with complete penetrance (100%) documented across multiple mice in both Naa10 KO lines. The data are supported by detailed skeletal analysis (Figure 2B, Table 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) with clear quantitative documentation. The homeotic transformation interpretation (C58, C60, C61) is reasonable given the consistent pattern of anteriorization across multiple vertebral segments, though these are inferences from anatomical observations.

results.result: Surviving Naa10-/Y mice develop progressive complications including hydronephrosis, genital defects, and hydrocephaly. Approximately 60% survive past 200 days, but ~40% of survivors develop clinically apparent hydrocephaly within the first three months. Hydronephrosis with ureteral thickening is observed as early as P3, and female Naa10-/- mice show decreased fecundity possibly due to hydrometrocolpos.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C70 provide quantitative longitudinal data (n=32 mice tracked, ~60% survival past 200 days, ~40% hydrocephaly incidence) with specific developmental timepoints. The observations are supported by CT scanning confirmation (C69) and histological evidence (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The speculation about ureteral vs. kidney defects (C65) and hydrometrocolpos causing decreased fecundity (C67) are appropriately qualified as speculative hypotheses requiring further investigation.

results.result: Naa10-/Y MEFs show no major global impairment in amino-terminal acetylation, with 98% of N-termini sites showing less than 10% variation compared to wildtype. Naa15 expression remains normal in Naa10 KO tissues, and a physical complex of Naa15 with undefined partners retaining NatA activity can be isolated from Naa10 KO tissues, suggesting the NatA complex remains active despite Naa10 loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 present rigorous mass spectrometry data (n=533 N-termini sites analyzed, 98% showing <10% variation) with both standard and stringent analysis criteria. Claims C77-C78 provide biochemical evidence (Figure 3B-C) demonstrating Naa15 expression and NatA activity in Naa10 KO tissues. The inference (C79) that NatA remains active is well-supported by the combined proteomics and biochemical data, though the identity of the compensating partner(s) is not yet determined.

results.result: Naa12 (Gm16286) is a previously unannotated Naa10-like paralog on chromosome 18 with >80% sequence identity to Naa10 and ~90% identity to Naa11. Naa12 is expressed in multiple tissues (confirmed by qPCR) and possesses intrinsic N-terminal acetyltransferase activity, as demonstrated by in vitro acetylation of acidic N-terminal peptides. Unlike Naa11, Naa12 is expressed in heart and other tissues beyond testis.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C88-C95 describe the discovery and characterization of Naa12 with multiple lines of evidence: bioinformatics identification (C88-C89, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), sequence analysis (C90-C91, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), expression confirmation by qPCR in multiple tissues (C92-C93, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and functional validation through in vitro enzymatic assays (C94-C95, Figure 4A). The discovery is novel and well-documented, representing a major finding that explains the lack of embryonic lethality in Naa10 KO mice.

results.result: Naa12 forms a stable complex with Naa15 and exhibits NatA catalytic activity. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate that Naa12 (along with Naa10 isoforms and Naa11) co-precipitates with V5-Naa15. Mass spectrometry identified five unique Naa12 peptides in Naa15 immunoprecipitates from Naa10 KO mouse livers, and the Naa12-Naa15 complex shows detectable amino-terminal acetylation activity toward NatA substrate peptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 provide multiple complementary lines of evidence: co-IP experiments in HEK293 cells (C96-C97, Figure 4B), mass spectrometry identification of five unique Naa12 peptides with higher intensities in Naa15 IPs (C100-C102, Table 2), and enzymatic activity assays (C98-C99, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F). The peptides are confirmed as unique to Naa12 in the mouse genome (C101), and no Naa10 peptides were detected in Naa10 KO samples (C103), validating the specificity of the findings.

results.result: Naa12 genetically compensates for Naa10 loss in mice. Naa12 single knockout mice are viable with no obvious phenotypes, but Naa10/Naa12 double knockout males (Naa10-/Y Naa12-/-) exhibit complete embryonic lethality, with no live births observed and zero embryos detected at E10.5 or E18.5. Compound heterozygous females (Naa10+/- Naa12-/-) also show embryonic lethality, and Naa10-/Y Naa12+/- males show reduced survival with developmental delays and degeneration by E10.5.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C11, C104-C121, C145 provide comprehensive genetic evidence for compensation through systematic breeding experiments with detailed genotyping at multiple developmental stages (E8.5, E10.5, E12.5, E18.5, postnatal). The complete absence of Naa10-/Y Naa12-/- males at all stages examined (C109, C111, C113) with quantitative data on resorptions (C112: n=23 at E18.5) and the reduced litter sizes (C110, C120, Table 3) strongly support the compensatory role. The data are presented in Figure 6 and supplementary figures with appropriate statistical modeling.

results.result: Compound heterozygous Naa10+/- Naa12+/- females show reduced survival below Mendelian ratios and smaller body size, with statistical modeling revealing that both Naa10 and Naa12 KOs significantly reduce weight when modeled together. The interaction of heterozygous Naa10 and Naa12 KOs significantly affects both weight and growth rate, suggesting Naa10 is the more dominant function but that two copies are required to replace complete Naa12 loss in females, possibly due to X-linked inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123 present primary observational data (Figure 6, Figure 7D) showing reduced survival and size. Claims C131-C133 provide rigorous statistical analysis demonstrating significant main effects and interactions using appropriate models (GEEs). The inference about Naa10 dominance (C124) is supported by the differential survival patterns across genotypes. The speculation about X-linked inactivation (C125-C126) is appropriately qualified and provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for the sex-specific effects observed.

results.result: Naa12 knockout alone does not significantly affect weight or growth rate in either male or female mice, whether heterozygous or homozygous, and shows no significant interaction with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C129 and C136 are based on rigorous statistical analysis using GEEs with appropriate controls for repeated measurements. The lack of significant effects for Naa12 KO alone contrasts with the significant effects observed for Naa10 KO and the interaction effects when both genes are affected, supporting the interpretation that Naa12 plays a compensatory rather than primary role.

results.result: The skeletal phenotypes observed in Naa10 KO mice overlap with some phenotypes found in humans with Ogden syndrome, including supernumerary vertebrae and hydrocephaly. The complete penetrance of supernumerary ribs in mice and their presence in some patients suggests a common pathway altered by NAA10 mutations. The skeletal findings are consistent with a homeotic anterior transformation hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C141, C174, and C192 represent reasonable inferences based on comparison of mouse phenotypes with documented human clinical features. The complete penetrance in mice (100%) combined with documented cases in human patients (C168-C171) supports a conserved pathway. The homeotic transformation interpretation (C192) is consistent with the pattern of anteriorization across multiple vertebral segments and comparison to other mutant mice with similar phenotypes (C175-C189). However, these are comparative inferences rather than direct mechanistic demonstrations.

results.result: Clinical features in Ogden syndrome probands, including large fontanels, ventricular dilatation, respiratory depression, and hypotonia/hypertonia, could be consistent with mild hydrocephaly that resolved over time. One OS patient's sequence of events (intraventricular hemorrhage, hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, ventriculo-peritoneal shunt) is possibly compatible with hydrocephaly requiring shunt placement.
results.evaluation: Claims C161 and C164 represent retrospective reinterpretation of previously published clinical data in light of the mouse findings. While the mouse model clearly shows hydrocephaly (C68-C70), the reinterpretation of human clinical features is speculative and based on limited clinical information from the literature. The claims are appropriately qualified with terms like "could be consistent" and "is possible," but lack prospective clinical validation or systematic re-evaluation of OS patients.

results.result: The phenotypes in Naa10 KO mice could be due to loss of Naa10-specific N-ε-acetyl-activity or non-catalytic roles of Naa10, or alternatively, differential quantitative expression of Naa10 and Naa12 within or between tissues might explain the phenotypic differences between single and compound mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C156 are explicitly speculative hypotheses proposed to explain the observed phenotypes in the context of globally intact N-terminal acetylation (C71). While these are plausible mechanistic explanations supported by literature citations (C153-C154), they remain untested hypotheses. The manuscript appropriately qualifies these as speculation, and they represent reasonable directions for future investigation rather than supported conclusions.

results.result: The maternal effect lethality rate in matings of Naa10-/- females with WT males was 29% in the first 24 hours and 36% in the first three days in this study, substantially lower than the 90% rate reported by Lee et al. 2017. Differences in survival might be due to maternal care differences or different combinations of modifying alleles in different C57BL/6J substrain genetic backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claim C197 presents quantitative data comparing this study's findings (36% death rate, n=127 pups) with prior literature (90% rate, n=51 pups), showing a substantial discrepancy. The proposed explanations (C198-C199) are speculative and appropriately qualified. The larger sample size in the current study (127 vs 51) provides more statistical power, but the true explanation for the discrepancy remains unclear. The genetic background hypothesis (C199) is plausible but untested, and the maternal care hypothesis (C198) would require behavioral studies not performed.
